note: Both warn against desire for beauty and her eyelids; Greek-English adds 'do not be hunted by your own eyes', and lacks KJV's 'in thine heart'.
cause: The Septuagint adds the clause about one's own eyes, absent from the Hebrew followed by the KJV.

note: KJV says a whore brings a man 'to a piece of bread' and the adulteress hunts life; Greek-English says 'a prostitute's price is as much as one loaf' and 'a woman hunts men's precious lives'.
cause: The compressed Hebrew allows both readings; the KJV reads reduction to bread, the Septuagint a price.

note: Both ask whether fire can be held in the bosom without burning clothes; KJV says 'take fire', Greek-English 'bind fire'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'take', where the Septuagint reads 'bind'; the difference is a nuance.

note: Both ask whether one can walk on hot coals without burning the feet; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both say the one who goes in to another's wife will not be innocent; KJV says 'his neighbour's wife', Greek-English 'a married woman' and applies non-acquittal to him and anyone touching her.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'neighbour's wife', where the Septuagint reads 'married woman'; the difference is slight.

note: KJV says 'Men do not despise a thief' who steals when hungry; Greek-English says 'It is no wonder if someone is caught stealing', changing the point from contempt to being caught.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'do not despise', where the Septuagint reads 'no wonder if caught'.

note: Both require sevenfold repayment and the loss of all goods; Greek-English adds 'he will rescue himself', while KJV says 'all the substance of his house'.
cause: The Septuagint adds the result of rescuing oneself, absent from the Hebrew followed by the KJV.

note: Both say the adulterer lacks understanding and destroys his own soul; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both promise injury, dishonor and lasting reproach; KJV has singular 'A wound and dishonour', Greek-English plural 'pains and dishonors' and 'never'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew singulars, where the Septuagint reads plurals and 'for ever'; the difference is slight.

note: Both describe jealous anger that will not spare; KJV says 'the rage of a man' and 'the day of vengeance', Greek-English 'her husband's anger' and 'the day of judgment'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'a man' and 'vengeance', where the Septuagint reads 'her husband' and 'judgment'.

note: Both say no ransom or many gifts will appease the husband; KJV says he will not 'rest content', Greek-English he will not 'trade his enmity' or 'be reconciled'.
cause: The Septuagint names the enmity and reconciliation explicitly; the differences are lexical choices.

note: Both bid the son keep the father's words and store up his commandments; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both say keeping the commandments gives life and liken the teaching to the eye's pupil; KJV says 'my law', Greek-English 'my words'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'instruction', where the Septuagint reads 'words'; the difference is slight.

note: Both bid binding the teachings on the fingers and writing them on the heart's tablet; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both make wisdom the learner's sister; KJV has direct address 'Thou art my sister' and 'call understanding thy kinswoman', Greek-English indirect speech and 'acquire understanding'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew direct address and 'call', where the Septuagint reads indirect speech and 'acquire'.

note: Both say wisdom keeps the son from the strange woman's flattering words; Greek-English adds 'wicked' and a conditional 'if she catches you'.
cause: The Septuagint adds 'wicked' and recasts the clause as a condition; the differences are slight.

note: KJV has the narrator say 'at the window of my house I looked'; Greek-English has the woman, 'she leans out from a window of her house'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew first-person observer, where the Septuagint makes the woman the observer.

note: Both single out a young man lacking sense among the simple; KJV has the narrator 'beheld' and 'discerned', Greek-English 'whoever she sees'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew first-person narrator, where the Septuagint continues with the woman as observer.

note: Both place the young man passing near her corner; KJV adds 'he went the way to her house', which Greek-English lacks, reading 'the passages of her houses'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew clause of walking toward her house, which the Septuagint lacks.

note: Both set the scene in evening darkness; KJV piles up 'twilight', 'evening' and 'black and dark night', while Greek-English adds the young man 'talking' and the night being 'still'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew series of darkness expressions; the Septuagint adds the talking and the night's stillness.

note: A woman in a harlot's attire meets him in both; KJV calls her 'subtil of heart', Greek-English says she makes 'young men's hearts fly away'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew description of her guarded heart, while the Septuagint describes her effect on young men's hearts instead.

note: Both describe her restless feet; KJV calls her 'loud and stubborn', Greek-English 'fluttering with excitement and dissolute'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'noisy and rebellious', where the Septuagint uses an image of excitement and dissipation.

note: Both alternate her outside and in the streets or squares, lying in wait at every corner; Greek-English adds that she 'roams' outside.
cause: The Septuagint makes the roaming explicit where the Hebrew followed by the KJV is more compressed; otherwise the difference is English wording.

note: Both have her seize him, kiss him and speak with an impudent or shameless face; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: KJV has plural 'peace offerings' and says she 'payed' her vows today; Greek-English has a single 'peace sacrifice' and says she is 'paying' them.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew plural and completed sense; the Septuagint's singular and present tense are a different construction.

note: Both have her come out to meet him and find him; KJV says 'diligently to seek thy face', Greek-English 'longing for your face'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'seek earnestly', where the Septuagint expresses desire; this is a lexical difference of nuance.

note: Both describe decking the bed with Egyptian textiles; KJV names 'tapestry', 'carved works' and 'fine linen', Greek-English 'bands' and 'double-sided rugs'.
cause: The KJV renders the difficult Hebrew textile terms, while the Septuagint names different furnishings; the Hebrew words remain uncertain.

note: KJV perfumes the bed with 'myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon'; Greek-English sprinkles the bed with 'saffron' and the house with cinnamon.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew list of spices, while the Septuagint names saffron and assigns the cinnamon to the house.

note: Both invite love until morning; KJV says 'take our fill' and 'solace ourselves with loves', Greek-English repeats 'come here' and says 'roll in love'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew image of drinking one's fill and delight; the Septuagint repeats the invitation and uses a different image.

note: Both say the husband is away on a long journey; KJV calls him 'the goodman', Greek-English 'my husband'.
cause: The KJV renders the Hebrew 'the man' as 'goodman', where the Septuagint makes 'my husband' explicit; the difference is slight.

note: Both have him take money; KJV says he will return 'at the day appointed', Greek-English 'after many days', and adds that the pouch is 'in his hand'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew appointed day (possibly the full moon), where the Septuagint reads only 'after many days'.

note: KJV says her 'fair speech' made him yield and her 'flattering' lips forced him; Greek-English says she 'led him astray' and drove him off course with 'snares' from her lips.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew smooth speech and lips, while the Septuagint introduces the images of straying and snares.

note: Both compare him to an ox to the slaughter; KJV adds 'a fool to the correction of the stocks', Greek-English 'a dog to bonds', and says he was 'made a fool'.

note: Both have a dart in the liver and a bird hurrying to the snare unaware of the cost; Greek-English applies the arrow to 'a deer', which the KJV lacks.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, which has no deer; the Septuagint introduces the deer into the comparison.

note: Both summon the hearer to attend to the speaker's words; KJV addresses plural 'children', Greek-English a single 'son'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew plural 'sons', where the Septuagint has the singular.

note: Both warn the heart not to turn aside to her ways; KJV adds 'go not astray in her paths', which Greek-English lacks.

note: Both say she has cast down many; KJV says 'many strong men have been slain', Greek-English that those she murdered are 'beyond counting'.
cause: The KJV takes the Hebrew word as 'mighty', while the Septuagint takes it in the sense of 'numerous'; the Hebrew allows either.

note: Both identify her house with the way to hell or Hades descending to the chambers of death; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: KJV asks whether wisdom and understanding do not cry out; Greek-English commands the hearer to proclaim wisdom so that understanding may heed them.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, where Wisdom calls; the Septuagint makes the addressee the one who proclaims.

note: Both place her on the high places and among the paths; KJV adds 'by the way', and Greek-English says she 'stands between' the paths.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew mention of the road; the remaining differences are a slightly different construction.

note: KJV has her 'cry' at the gates, the city entry and the doors; Greek-English has her 'sit' beside the gates 'of rulers' and be 'praised' at the entrances.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, where she cries out at the city gate; the Septuagint reads rulers and a passive verb of praise.

note: Both have Wisdom call to men and direct her voice to the sons of man; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: KJV tells the 'simple' to understand 'wisdom' and 'fools' to be of an understanding heart; Greek-English has 'innocent ones', 'resourcefulness', 'uneducated' and 'put your heart into it'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew terms; the Septuagint's words carry somewhat different nuances.

note: Both promise excellent or noble speech; KJV says 'the opening of my lips' shall be right things, Greek-English that she will 'bring forth' upright things from her lips.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'opening of my lips', where the Septuagint uses a verb of bringing forth; a slightly different construction.

note: KJV says her mouth 'shall speak truth' and 'wickedness' is an abomination to her lips; Greek-English says her throat will 'meditate' on truth and 'lying lips' are detestable before her.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'wickedness' and 'my lips', where the Septuagint names lying lips as the object of abhorrence.

note: Both say all the words of her mouth are in righteousness with nothing 'froward or perverse', or 'crooked or entangled', in them; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both say her words are plain to the one who understands and right to those who find knowledge; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both prefer instruction to silver and knowledge to choice gold; Greek-English adds a third clause, 'choose discernment rather than pure gold', which the KJV lacks.
cause: The KJV follows the shorter Hebrew; the third clause is an addition in the Septuagint.

note: Both rank wisdom above precious things; KJV says 'rubies' and 'all the things that may be desired', Greek-English 'costly stones' and 'nothing precious'.
cause: The KJV renders the uncertain Hebrew gem word as 'rubies', where the Septuagint has 'costly stones'; a lexical difference of nuance.

note: KJV has Wisdom dwell with 'prudence' and 'find out knowledge of witty inventions'; Greek-English has her dwell in 'counsel' and 'call upon knowledge and reflection'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'shrewdness' and 'find', where the Septuagint reads 'counsel' and 'called upon'.

note: Both make the fear of the Lord hate pride, arrogance and evil ways; KJV ends with 'the froward mouth', Greek-English with 'the perverted ways of evil people'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'perverse mouth', where the Septuagint reads 'perverted ways'; the opening construction is a lexical choice.

note: Both claim counsel and strength; KJV has 'sound wisdom' and 'I am understanding', Greek-English has 'security' and 'understanding is mine'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew identification of the speaker with understanding; the Septuagint reads 'security' and possession instead.

note: Both say kings reign through Wisdom; KJV says princes 'decree justice', Greek-English that rulers 'write righteousness'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'decree', where the Septuagint uses 'write'; a lexical difference of nuance.

note: KJV says princes, nobles and 'all the judges of the earth' rule by Wisdom; Greek-English says 'great men become great' and 'sovereigns rule the earth'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew reference to judges, while the Septuagint speaks of magnates and sovereigns.

note: Both say Wisdom loves those who love her and is found by those who seek her; KJV says those who seek her 'early'.
cause: The KJV renders the Hebrew verb as seeking 'early', a nuance the Septuagint's plain 'seek' does not carry.

note: Both place riches, honour or glory and righteousness with Wisdom; KJV speaks of 'durable riches', Greek-English of 'possession of many things'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'lasting wealth', where the Septuagint emphasises abundance; a lexical difference of nuance.

note: KJV says her 'fruit' is better than gold and 'fine gold'; Greek-English says it is better 'to reap' her than gold and 'precious stone'. Both prefer her yield to choice silver.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew pair of gold terms, where the Septuagint reads 'precious stone' and makes Wisdom herself the harvest.

note: Both place Wisdom in the ways of righteousness and the paths of judgment; KJV says she 'leads', Greek-English that she 'walks' and 'moves'.
cause: The KJV renders the Hebrew verb as 'lead' where the Septuagint has 'walk'; a lexical difference of nuance.

note: Both have Wisdom give substance to those who love her and fill their treasures; Greek-English adds 'with good things'.
cause: The Septuagint makes the contents of the storehouses explicit; the KJV follows the shorter Hebrew.

note: Both place Wisdom's establishment before the age, in the beginning; KJV adds 'or ever the earth was', which Greek-English places in its next verse, and says 'set up' where Greek-English says 'founded'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew verse division and 'installed'; the Septuagint arranges the earth clause into 8:24 and reads 'founded'.

note: Both mention depths and springs before creation; KJV says 'I was brought forth', while Greek-English instead adds 'before making the earth' to its continuing sentence.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew; the Septuagint arranges the clauses differently and lacks the birth statement here.

note: Both place Wisdom's birth before the mountains and hills; KJV says 'was I brought forth', Greek-English 'He gives me birth', naming the agent and using the present.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew passive past, where the Septuagint uses an active present verb; a difference of construction and tense.

note: KJV continues the 'not yet' setting, before he had made the earth, fields and dust; Greek-English positively asserts that the Lord made countries, uninhabited places and the inhabited extremities.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'not yet' clause, while the Septuagint reads a positive statement of creation.

note: Both place Wisdom present when he prepared the heavens; KJV has him set 'a compass upon the face of the depth', Greek-English 'His own throne upon winds'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew circle over the deep, while the Septuagint reads a different cosmological image.

note: Both describe establishing the clouds above and strengthening springs; KJV names 'the fountains of the deep', Greek-English 'the springs of the world beneath heaven'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'deep', where the Septuagint reads 'beneath heaven'.

note: Both mention the foundations of the earth; KJV also has the decree to the sea that the waters should not pass his commandment, which Greek-English lacks.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew sea-boundary clause, which has no counterpart in the Septuagint.

note: Both place Wisdom beside him, his daily delight, rejoicing before him; KJV calls her 'one brought up with him', Greek-English 'fitting things together'.
cause: The KJV takes the disputed Hebrew 'amon' as a nursling, while the Septuagint renders it as one who harmonises or fits together.

note: KJV keeps Wisdom rejoicing in the habitable earth with her delights among men; Greek-English makes God rejoice after completing the world and delight in humankind.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew with Wisdom as subject, while the Septuagint shifts the rejoicing to the divine maker.

note: Both call the hearer to listen; KJV addresses 'children' and adds 'blessed are they that keep my ways', which Greek-English has only in 8:34, addressing one 'son'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew; the Septuagint omits the blessing here and places it within 8:34, with a singular address.

note: Both bless the one who listens, watching daily at her gates and posts; Greek-English adds 'the person who will keep my ways', which the KJV has at 8:32.
cause: The Septuagint places the keeping-of-ways blessing in this verse, while the KJV follows the Hebrew placement at 8:32.

note: KJV says whoever 'findeth me findeth life' and obtains the LORD's favour; Greek-English says her 'ways out are ways out to life' and favour 'is prepared' by the Lord.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'finding', while the Septuagint reads 'ways out' and a passive construction for favour.

note: Both say sinning against Wisdom harms one's own soul and those hating her love death; KJV has a singular sinner who 'wrongeth' his soul, Greek-English plural sinners who 'act impiously'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew singular; the Septuagint's plural and stronger verb are a different construction.

note: Both have Wisdom build her house with seven pillars; KJV says she 'hewn out' the pillars, Greek-English that she 'set' them beneath it.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'hewn', where the Septuagint describes their placement; a lexical difference of nuance.

note: Both have Wisdom kill animals, mix wine and furnish her table; Greek-English calls the beasts 'sacrificial animals' and adds 'in a mixing-bowl'.
cause: The Septuagint makes the sacrificial sense and the bowl explicit where the Hebrew followed by the KJV is plainer.

note: Both have Wisdom send attendants and call out; KJV sends 'maidens' and has her cry 'upon the highest places of the city', Greek-English sends 'servants' with a 'lofty proclamation' summoning 'to the mixing-bowl'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew female attendants and city heights, while the Septuagint reads a proclamation to the mixing-bowl.

note: Both invite the simple or foolish to turn in and address those lacking understanding; Greek-English says 'turn aside to me' and 'foolish' where the KJV says 'simple'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'simple'; the Septuagint's 'foolish' and 'to me' are slight lexical differences.

note: Both invite guests to eat her bread and drink the wine she mixed; Greek-English adds 'for you' and has plural 'loaves'.
cause: The Septuagint adds the short phrase 'for you'; the remaining difference is English wording.

note: Both urge leaving folly to live; KJV adds 'go in the way of understanding', while Greek-English has 'seek understanding, so that you may live' and 'set insight right in knowledge'.
cause: The KJV follows the shorter Hebrew; the Septuagint expands the verse with additional clauses.

note: Both say the reprover brings disgrace on himself; KJV names 'a scorner' and 'a wicked man', Greek-English 'evil people' and 'an impious person'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'scorner', where the Septuagint speaks of evil people; the remaining differences are English wording.

note: Both contrast the hatred of the rebuked with the love of a reproved wise person; KJV warns against reproving 'a scorner', Greek-English 'evil people'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'scorner', while the Septuagint generalises to evil people.

note: Both say teaching the wise and just makes them wiser; KJV gives 'instruction', Greek-English 'a starting point', and KJV says he will 'increase in learning', Greek-English 'receive still more'.

note: Both promise longer days and added years; KJV says this comes 'by me', Wisdom, while Greek-English says 'in this way'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'by me', where the Septuagint reads 'in this way'.

note: Both say wisdom profits oneself and the opposite is borne alone; Greek-English adds 'Son' and 'wise for your neighbors', and contrasts becoming 'evil' where the KJV says 'scornest'.
cause: The KJV follows the shorter Hebrew; the Septuagint adds the address and the benefit to neighbours.

note: KJV calls the foolish woman 'clamorous', 'simple' and knowing nothing; Greek-English says the brazen woman 'comes to lack a morsel' and does not know shame.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew description of noisy ignorance, while the Septuagint reads a different statement about want and shamelessness.

note: Both seat her at the door of her house; KJV puts her seat 'in the high places of the city', Greek-English 'openly in the squares'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'heights of the city', where the Septuagint names the public squares.

note: Both have her call to passers-by who go straight on their ways; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both invite the simple to turn in; Greek-English says 'most foolish' 'among you' and shifts to a first-person 'I urge', where the KJV has 'she saith'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, repeating 9:4; the Septuagint uses a superlative and a first-person verb.

note: Both commend stolen water and secret bread; KJV states that they are sweet and pleasant, Greek-English commands 'Taste' them, with bread and water in reverse order.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew statement, where the Septuagint uses an imperative; a difference of construction.

note: Both say he does not know the deadly outcome; KJV says 'the dead are there' and her guests are 'in the depths of hell', Greek-English 'earth-born ones perish' and he comes upon 'the ledge of Hades'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'shades' and 'depths', while the Septuagint reads 'earth-born ones' and a different image of Hades.

note: Both contrast the wise son who gladdens his father with the foolish son who grieves his mother; KJV opens with the heading 'The proverbs of Solomon', which Greek-English lacks.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew collection heading, which is absent from the Septuagint.

note: Both say righteousness delivers from death; KJV says 'treasures of wickedness profit nothing', Greek-English that treasures 'will not profit lawless people'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'treasures of wickedness', where the Septuagint makes lawless people the ones not profited.

note: Both say the Lord will not let the righteous starve; KJV says he casts away 'the substance' of the wicked, Greek-English that he overturns their 'life'.
cause: The KJV renders the Hebrew 'craving' as 'substance', while the Septuagint reads 'life'; the object differs.

note: KJV says one becomes poor through a 'slack hand' and the 'diligent' grow rich; Greek-English says 'poverty humbles a man' and the 'courageous' make rich.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew cause of poverty, where the Septuagint describes poverty's effect and reads 'courageous'.

note: KJV contrasts the wise son who 'gathereth in summer' with the son who 'sleepeth in harvest'; Greek-English says an intelligent son is 'preserved from scorching heat' and a lawless son 'ruined by wind'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew about gathering and sleeping, while the Septuagint reads different actions and outcomes.

note: Both put blessing on the head of the just; Greek-English names it 'the Lord's' blessing, and says 'untimely mourning' covers the mouth of the wicked where the KJV says 'violence'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'violence', where the Septuagint reads 'untimely mourning' and adds the Lord.

note: Both praise the memory of the just; KJV says the name of the wicked 'shall rot', Greek-English that it 'is extinguished'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew image of decay, where the Septuagint uses extinguishing; a different nuance.

note: Both say the wise in heart receive commands; KJV says 'a prating fool shall fall', Greek-English 'the unrestrained person who twists things with his lips will be tripped up'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'fool of lips', which the Septuagint expands with lack of restraint and crooked speech.

note: Both contrast the secure walk of the upright with the exposure of one who perverts his ways; the differences are English wording.
cause: The difference is one of English wording; the KJV and Greek-English agree here.

note: Both say winking or signalling with the eye causes sorrow; KJV ends 'a prating fool shall fall', Greek-English 'one who reproves with frankness makes peace' and adds 'deceitfully'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, repeating 10:8b; the Septuagint has a different second clause.

note: KJV calls the mouth of the righteous a well of life, Greek-English says a fountain of life is in their 'hand'; KJV has 'violence' and Greek-English 'destruction' covering the mouth of the wicked.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'mouth' and 'violence', where the Septuagint reads 'hand' and 'destruction'.

note: Both say hatred stirs up strife; KJV says love covers 'all sins', Greek-English that friendship covers 'all who do not love strife'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'offences', while the Septuagint gives the covering a different object.

note: KJV has two clauses: wisdom found in the lips of the understanding, and a rod for the back of the senseless; Greek-English merges them so the wise speaker 'strikes' the man lacking heart.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew parallel clauses, while the Septuagint restructures them into one statement with the wise as agent.

note: Both oppose the wise who store knowledge to the foolish mouth near ruin; KJV says 'lay up knowledge', Greek-English 'hide discernment', and the fool is 'rash' in Greek-English.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'store up'; the Septuagint's 'hide' and 'rash' are lexical differences of nuance.

note: Both call the rich man's wealth a strong city; KJV says poverty is the destruction of 'the poor', Greek-English of 'the impious'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'poor', where the Septuagint reads 'impious'.

note: Both say the labour or works of the righteous lead to life and the fruit of the wicked to sin; Greek-English has plural 'fruits' and 'sins' and the verb 'produce'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew singulars and 'tendeth to'; the Septuagint's plurals are a slight difference of construction.

note: KJV says the one who keeps instruction is in the way of life and the one refusing reproof errs; Greek-English makes 'discipline' itself guard the paths and 'unreproved' discipline wander.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew, where a person is the subject, while the Septuagint makes discipline the subject of both clauses.

note: KJV condemns one who hides hatred with 'lying lips' and the slanderer as fools; Greek-English says 'righteous lips' conceal enmity, condemning only those who bring forth abuse.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'lying lips', while the Septuagint reads 'righteous lips', reversing the evaluation of concealment.

note: Both say many words do not lack sin and restraint of the lips is wise; Greek-English addresses the hearer directly as 'you'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew third-person statement, where the Septuagint uses second-person address; a different construction.

note: Both liken the just tongue to choice silver; KJV says the wicked heart 'is little worth', Greek-English that it 'will fail', and calls the silver 'fire-tested'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew devaluation of the wicked heart, where the Septuagint predicts its failing.

note: KJV says the lips of the righteous 'feed many' and fools die 'for want of wisdom'; Greek-English says the lips 'know lofty things' and fools die 'in want'.
cause: The KJV follows the Hebrew 'feed' and 'lack of sense', while the Septuagint reads 'know lofty things' and leaves the want unspecified.

note: Both say the LORD's blessing makes rich without added sorrow; Greek-English adds that the blessing is 'upon the head of the righteous' and that the sorrow is 'in the heart'.
